### 1.  Use the exponential–Bessel expansion  

For any real \(z\),

\[
e^{z\cos x}=I_{0}(z)+2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}I_{n}(z)\cos(nx),
\]

where \(I_{n}\) is the modified Bessel function of the first kind.  
Putting \(z=1\),

\[
e^{\cos x}=I_{0}(1)+2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}I_{n}(1)\cos(nx).
\]

Hence

\[
\begin{aligned}
I&=\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\Bigl[I_{0}(1)+2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}I_{n}(1)\cos(nx)\Bigr]dx  \\
 &=\frac{\pi}{2}I_{0}(1)+2\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}I_{n}(1)\frac{\sin\!\bigl(n\pi/2\bigr)}{n}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(\sin(n\pi/2)=0\) for even \(n\) and equals
\(+1\) for \(n=4k+1\) and \(-1\) for \(n=4k+3\),

\[
I=\frac{\pi}{2}I_{0}(1)+2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\Bigl(\frac{I_{4k+1}(1)}{4k+1}-\frac{I_{4k+3}(1)}{4k+3}\Bigr).
\tag{1}
\]

---

### 2.  Recognise the modified Struve function  

The modified Struve function \(L_{0}(z)\) has the series representation  

\[
L_{0}(z)=2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\Bigl(\frac{I_{2k+1}(z)}{2k+1}-\frac{I_{2k+3}(z)}{2k+3}\Bigr),
\qquad z\in\mathbb{R}.
\]

Comparing this series with the sum in (1) we obtain  

\[
2\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\Bigl(\frac{I_{4k+1}(1)}{4k+1}-\frac{I_{4k+3}(1)}{4k+3}\Bigr)
=\frac{\pi}{2}L_{0}(1).
\]

Therefore

\[
I=\frac{\pi}{2}\Bigl[I_{0}(1)+L_{0}(1)\Bigr].
\tag{2}
\]

---

### 3.  Final result  

Equation (2) gives the value of the integral in terms of standard special functions:

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle 
\int_{0}^{\pi/2} e^{\cos x}\,dx
=\frac{\pi}{2}\,\Bigl[I_{0}(1)+L_{0}(1)\Bigr]}
\]

where  

* \(I_{0}(z)=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k}}{(k!)^{2}}\) is the modified Bessel function of the first kind,
* \(L_{0}(z)=\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(z/2)^{2k+1}}{\Gamma\!\bigl(k+\tfrac32\bigr)^{2}}\) is the modified Struve function of order 0.

A numerical evaluation gives  

\[
\int_{0}^{\pi/2} e^{\cos x}\,dx
\approx 3.10437901785555.
\]<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
